title: Neural networks and backpropagation
summary: Why stacking layers needs nonlinearity, what hidden units compute, and how backprop gets every gradient in one backward sweep: by hand, for softmax and mini-batches, in a tiny autograd engine, and on real digits.
outcomes: Explain why stacked linear layers collapse to one, and how ReLU hidden units build piecewise-linear functions and separable features
Compute a forward pass through a small MLP and its cross-entropy loss by hand
Backpropagate through a computational graph using local gradients and the add, multiply, max and fan-out rules
Apply the four backprop equations to get every weight gradient, and verify them with a gradient check
Derive the softmax cross-entropy gradient p minus one-hot(y) and compute log-softmax without overflow
Write backprop for a mini-batch in matrix form with the right shapes, transposes and reduction
Explain backprop's compute and memory cost and vanishing gradients, and build a small reverse-mode autograd engine
Train an MLP on handwritten digits and read its loss curves, test accuracy and confusion matrix

lessons.title: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR

blocks.md:
You already know how to fit a linear model $\hat y = w^\top x + b$ by gradient descent on a loss, where $w^\top x$ is the dot product of the weights with the input, the weighted sum $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots$. Linear models are easy to train, but they can only draw a straight **decision boundary**. To classify, you threshold the output (say, predict 1 when $\hat y > 0.5$), and the inputs where $w^\top x + b$ equals exactly 0.5 form a **hyperplane**: a straight line in 2D, a flat plane in 3D. Every input on one side gets one answer. Many real patterns are not like that.

The smallest example is **XOR** (exclusive or): the output is 1 when exactly one of two binary inputs is 1. The four points: (0,0) gives 0, (0,1) gives 1, (1,0) gives 1, (1,1) gives 0.

Fit the best linear model to those four points with squared error and you get $w = (0, 0)$ and $b = 0.5$: it predicts 0.5 for every input. Here is why. When $x_1 = 0$ the two targets are 0 and 1, and when $x_1 = 1$ they are 1 and 0, so either way they average 0.5: on its own, $x_1$ says nothing about the target, and the same holds for $x_2$. The four inputs cover every combination once, so the two inputs are uncorrelated and each weight is fitted on its own; both come out 0, and the bias becomes 0.5, the mean target. No straight line puts (0,1) and (1,0) on one side and (0,0) and (1,1) on the other, so the linear model gives up and outputs the average.

Historically this mattered: critics including Marvin Minsky pointed to the inability of linear models such as the **perceptron** (Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 model: one linear unit that outputs 1 when $w^\top x + b > 0$ and 0 otherwise) to learn XOR, which contributed to a backlash against neural network research.

blocks.prompt: Idea: stack two linear layers, $h = W_1 x + b_1$ then $\hat y = W_2 h + b_2$. The model now has more parameters and a hidden layer. Can it learn XOR?
blocks.reveal: No. Substitute one into the other: $\hat y = (W_2 W_1) x + (W_2 b_1 + b_2)$. That is a single matrix times $x$ plus a single bias, so it is still a linear model with exactly the same limits. Stacking any number of purely linear layers collapses into one linear layer.

blocks.tex: W_2(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2 = \underbrace{(W_2 W_1)}_{W'} x + \underbrace{(W_2 b_1 + b_2)}_{b'}
blocks.caption: An affine map is a matrix multiply plus a constant shift, like W x + b. Composing two of them gives another one, W' x + b'. Depth only helps if something nonlinear sits between the layers.

blocks.md:
The fix is a **nonlinear activation function** $g$ applied element by element after each linear step. A **neuron** (or unit) computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, $z = w^\top x + b$, then outputs $a = g(z)$. A **layer** is many neurons reading the same inputs, written $a = g(Wx + b)$. Layers between the input and the output are **hidden layers**, and a stack of them is a **feedforward network** or **multilayer perceptron (MLP)**.

The default modern choice for $g$ is the **rectified linear unit**, $\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)$. It is the identity for positive inputs, and *rectified* means negative inputs are cut to 0, like an electrical rectifier that lets current through in one direction only.

blocks.tex: f(x) = w^\top \max(0,\ W^\top x + c) + b,\quad W=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\ c=\begin{bmatrix}0\\-1\end{bmatrix},\ w=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix},\ b=0
blocks.caption: A hand-built XOR solution from Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, section 6.1: two hidden ReLU units, one output. In words: h1 = ReLU(x1 + x2), h2 = ReLU(x1 + x2 - 1), and the output is h1 - 2 h2.

blocks.title: Two ReLU units solve XOR

scenes.caption: The four XOR inputs and their targets. The best linear fit (least squares) outputs 0.5 everywhere here. Watch how two hidden units bend the space.
Linear step: both hidden units compute x1 + x2, and unit 2 adds bias -1. Now (0,1) and (1,0) land on the same values, but the map is still linear.
ReLU clips negatives to 0. Only h2 at (0,0) changes, from -1 to 0. This one bend is what the linear model could not do.
Output = h1 - 2 x h2. For (1,1): 2 - 2 = 0. For (0,0): 0 - 0 = 0. All four outputs now equal the targets exactly.

blocks.md: A hidden layer only adds power because of the nonlinearity between layers. Without it, any stack of layers is one linear map in disguise.

How far does this go? The **universal approximation theorem** says a feedforward network with one hidden layer of enough units (with ReLU or a **squashing** activation, an S-shaped function such as the sigmoid of lesson 3 that squeezes every input into a bounded range) can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as you like. It does not say how many units you need or that training will find the right weights. The next lesson shows the idea behind it with real numbers. In practice we stack several layers and *learn* the weights from data, which is where backpropagation comes in.

Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

blocks.question: In the XOR network above, replace ReLU with the identity function $g(z)=z$ and keep the same weights. What does the network output for input (0,0)?
options: 0, same as before
0.5, like the best linear fit
blocks.explain: Without the clip, h2 at (0,0) stays at -1, so output = h1 - 2 x h2 = 0 - 2 x (-1) = 2. The whole network becomes $-(x_1+x_2)+2$, a linear function that outputs 2, 1, 1, 0 on the four inputs.

blocks.question: A network has three hidden layers of 512 units each, but every activation is the identity. Which statement is true?
options: It can only represent affine functions of its input, same as a single linear layer
It can represent any continuous function given enough units
It can represent XOR but not more complex functions
It is equivalent to a single hidden layer network with ReLU
blocks.explain: Each layer is affine and the composition of affine maps is affine, so the whole stack collapses to $W'x+b'$. The extra parameters add cost but no expressive power.

lessons.title: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 ended with a promise: one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. To see why, start with a single ReLU unit reading one number $x$. Its output $\mathrm{ReLU}(x - s)$ is 0 until $x$ reaches $s$, then rises in a straight line. Plotted, it looks like a door **hinge**: flat, then bent at $s$. The unit's bias sets where the bend sits ($s$ is minus the bias over the weight) and the weight on the way out sets how steep the ramp is.

One hinge is not much. A sum of hinges is a **piecewise-linear** curve: straight pieces joined at bends, with each new hinge changing the slope at its own bend point.

blocks.tex: f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\, \mathrm{ReLU}(x - s_i), \qquad c_i = (\text{slope after } s_i) - (\text{slope before } s_i)
blocks.caption: A one-hidden-layer ReLU network with one input: n hidden units with bends at s_i, and output weights c_i that each add a change of slope.

blocks.md: Now approximate $\sin x$ on $[0, 2\pi]$. Pick $n + 1$ equally spaced points, read $\sin$ there, and connect the dots with $n$ straight pieces. Each piece needs one hinge: the first sets the starting slope and each later one adds the change in slope. The output weights $c_i$ are those slope changes, so the whole network is written down, not trained.

blocks.prompt: Try $n = 2$ pieces: bends at $0$ and $\pi$, joining the points $x = 0, \pi, 2\pi$. What does the 2-hinge network output, and what is its worst error against $\sin x$?
blocks.reveal: It outputs **0 everywhere**. All three points have $\sin x = 0$, so connecting them gives a flat line and the worst error is 1, at the peaks. Two hinges are not too few in principle; they are in the wrong places. Where the bends sit matters as much as how many there are, and training is what moves them.

blocks.title: Approximating sin x with ReLU hinges

scenes.caption: One ReLU unit: flat at 0 until the bend point s, then a straight ramp with slope c. Drag the sliders: the bias moves the bend, the output weight sets the slope.
2 pieces, bends at 0 and pi: every sample point has sin x = 0, so the sum of hinges is the flat line 0. Worst error 1.0.
4 pieces, bends every pi/2: the curve becomes a zigzag through the peaks. Worst error 0.21. (The hinge at pi gets weight 0 because the slope does not change there.)
8 pieces: worst error 0.070. 16 pieces bring it to 0.019. More hinges, smaller error, with no limit on how close you can get.

blocks.md: Measured on a fine grid, the worst-case errors are 1.0, 0.21, 0.070 and 0.019 for 2, 4, 8 and 16 pieces: past the first step, each doubling of hidden units cuts the error by roughly 3 to 4 times. This is the constructive idea behind universal approximation. Michael Nielsen's visual proof in *Neural Networks and Deep Learning* (chapter 4) builds the same kind of staircase from steep sigmoid steps paired into bumps. For ReLU, Goodfellow et al. cite Leshno et al. (1993): shallow networks with a broad family of non-polynomial activations, ReLU included, are universal approximators.

With two inputs, each hidden unit computes $\mathrm{ReLU}(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b)$. The set where $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = 0$ is a line, so each unit **cuts the plane**: it outputs 0 on one side and a ramp that grows with distance on the other. The output layer then adds these ramps with weights.

The XOR network from lesson 1 has two cuts, the parallel lines $x_1 + x_2 = 0$ (unit $h_1$) and $x_1 + x_2 = 1$ (unit $h_2$). Its output $h_1 - 2h_2$ is 0 below the first line, climbs to 1 at the second, and falls again beyond it: a ridge whose top runs through (0,1) and (1,0).

blocks.title: Two cuts make a ridge: the XOR network over the plane

scenes.caption: Unit h1 = ReLU(x1 + x2) on a grid (rows: x2, columns: x1). Zero in the lower-left corner, below the line x1 + x2 = 0, a ramp everywhere else. Boxed cells are the four XOR inputs.
Unit h2 = ReLU(x1 + x2 - 1): the same ramp with its cut shifted to the line x1 + x2 = 1. Of the XOR inputs, only (1,1) lies past it.
Output h1 - 2 h2: the second ramp, doubled, bends the first one back down. The result is a ridge of height 1 along x1 + x2 = 1, with 0 at (0,0) and (1,1). Red cells are negative.

blocks.md: There is a second way to read the same network. Treat the hidden activations $(h_1, h_2)$ as new coordinates for each input. The four XOR points land at (0,0), (1,0), (1,0) and (2,1): (0,1) and (1,0) merge, and in these coordinates one straight line separates the classes. The output unit is just a linear model, but it works on **features** the hidden layer computed instead of on raw inputs. Learning such features from data is called **representation learning**; the title of Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams's 1986 backprop paper, *Learning representations by back-propagating errors*, names exactly this.

blocks.title: The hidden layer moves the XOR points

scenes.caption: Input space. The two target-1 points, (0,1) and (1,0), sit on one diagonal and the target-0 points on the other, so no straight line separates them.

After the linear step only: (z1, z2) = (x1 + x2, x1 + x2 - 1). (0,1) and (1,0) land on the same point, and all three positions fall on one straight line, with the class 1 point in the middle. Still not separable.
After ReLU: (0, -1) is clipped to (0, 0) and the line is broken. Now the line h1 - 2 h2 = 0.5 separates the classes: the output h1 - 2 h2 is 1 for the middle point and 0 for the other two.

blocks.md: Why stack layers if one is enough? The catch in the theorem is size. Goodfellow et al. (section 6.4.1) report results where some families of functions need exponentially many hidden units in a single layer but far fewer when the network is deep. Montufar et al. (2014) count the **linear regions** of a ReLU network (the pieces on which it is linear) and show that their maximum number can grow exponentially with depth. The intuition: each layer can fold the space produced by the layer before it, like folding paper, so later layers reuse earlier pieces many times. The book adds a caution: there is no guarantee that the functions we care about have this repeated structure.

A ReLU hidden unit is a hinge (one input) or a cut with a ramp (many inputs). The output layer adds these up into a piecewise-linear function, and equivalently, it runs a linear model on the features the hidden layer computed.

Misconception: universal approximation means one wide layer is all you need. It says suitable weights exist, not how many units that takes or that gradient descent will find them. The notes of CS231n, Stanford's course on convolutional neural networks for visual recognition, call it mathematically cute but a relatively weak statement in practice.

blocks.question: Connect-the-dots approximation of $\sin x$ gave worst errors 0.21, 0.070 and 0.019 with 4, 8 and 16 equal pieces. Roughly how many pieces give a worst error near 0.005?
blocks.explain: Each doubling cut the error by about 3 to 4 times, and the ratio was heading toward 4. One more doubling, to 32 pieces, gives about 0.0048. 64 would overshoot to around 0.0012.

blocks.question: In the XOR network the output unit is $h_1 - 2h_2$, a purely linear function of the hidden activations. How can it classify XOR, which no linear model can?
options: The hidden layer remaps the inputs into features where a straight line separates the classes; the output unit is linear in those features, not in $x$
The output unit secretly applies a ReLU too
It cannot; it only fits the four points by memorizing them
Because the weights were trained, not chosen by hand
blocks.explain: Linear in $h$ does not mean linear in $x$. After ReLU the points sit at (0,0), (1,0) and (2,1) in hidden space, where the line $h_1 - 2h_2 = 0.5$ separates them. The weights here were set by hand, so training is not the reason.

lessons.title: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies

blocks.md:
We number layers $l = 1, \dots, L$ and call the input $a^0 = x$. The superscript is a layer number, not an exponent: when you hear a to the power 2, or a squared, it means layer 2's activations. Each layer does two things: a linear step that produces the **pre-activation** $z^l$, then the activation function that produces the **activation** $a^l$. Running these steps from input to output is the **forward pass**.

If layer $l$ has $n_l$ units, its weight matrix $W^l$ has shape $n_l \times n_{l-1}$: row $j$ holds the weights into unit $j$, and entry $W^l_{jk}$ connects unit $k$ of the previous layer to unit $j$.

blocks.tex: z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l, \qquad a^l = g(z^l)
blocks.caption: One layer of a feedforward network. The output layer often uses a different g, chosen to match the loss.

blocks.md:
Common activation functions:

- **Sigmoid** $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ squashes to (0, 1). Its derivative is $\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$, at most 0.25 (at $z=0$).
- **tanh**, the hyperbolic tangent $\tanh z = (e^z - e^{-z})/(e^z + e^{-z})$, squashes to (-1, 1), centred on 0. It is a rescaled sigmoid, $\tanh z = 2\sigma(2z) - 1$, and its derivative $1-\tanh^2 z$ peaks at 1, at $z = 0$.
- **ReLU** $\max(0,z)$ has derivative 1 for $z>0$ and 0 for $z<0$.

Goodfellow et al. call ReLU the default recommendation for hidden layers in modern networks. Keep an eye on the derivatives: lesson 9 shows why they matter.

blocks.caption: Where the sigmoid slope comes from: differentiate 1 over 1 plus e to the minus z, then split the result into sigma times 1 minus sigma.

blocks.md: Step by step: by the chain rule, the derivative of $1/(1+e^{-z})$ is $e^{-z}/(1+e^{-z})^2$. Split it into two factors: $1/(1+e^{-z})$, which is $\sigma(z)$, and $e^{-z}/(1+e^{-z})$, which equals $1 - \sigma(z)$. So the slope is $p(1-p)$ with $p = \sigma(z)$, a product of two numbers that add up to 1, $p$ and $1 - p$. It is largest when both are 0.5, giving 0.25 at $z = 0$. When $z$ is far from 0 in either direction, $p$ is pinned near 0 or 1, the slope is near 0, and the unit is called **saturated**: it passes almost no gradient back.

blocks.title: Activation functions and their slopes

scenes.caption: Sigmoid and its slope. The slope peaks at only 0.25 and is near 0 once |z| is above about 5: a saturated unit passes almost no gradient back.
tanh is a rescaled sigmoid centred on 0. Its slope peaks at 1, larger than sigmoid's, but it also saturates for large |z|.
ReLU is the identity for z > 0 and zero otherwise. Its slope is exactly 1 on the positive side, so it does not saturate there; units stuck at z < 0 get zero gradient.

blocks.md: Here is the network we will use for the rest of the course: 2 inputs, 2 sigmoid hidden units, 1 sigmoid output, so 9 parameters: a 2 x 2 weight matrix and 2 biases into the hidden layer, then 2 weights and 1 bias into the output. One training example: $x = (1.0, 0.5)$ with label $y = 1$. The output $a^2$ is read as the probability that $y=1$, and the loss is **binary cross-entropy**, $L = -[y \ln a^2 + (1-y)\ln(1-a^2)]$, the negative log-likelihood you met with logistic regression. With $y = 1$ the second term vanishes, so here the loss is just $-\ln a^2$.

blocks.caption: Starting weights for the worked example (chosen by hand so the numbers are easy to follow).

blocks.title: Forward pass through a 2-2-1 network

scenes.caption: Edge labels are the weights. Each hidden unit will take a weighted sum of x1 and x2, add its bias, then apply the sigmoid.
h2: z = 0.2 x 1.0 + 0.8 x 0.5 - 0.1 = 0.50, so a = sigmoid(0.50) = 0.622. Both hidden units can be computed in parallel: this is one matrix multiply.
Output: z = 0.7 x 0.611 - 0.4 x 0.622 + 0.2 = 0.378, so the predicted probability is sigmoid(0.378) = 0.594.
Loss = -ln(0.594) = 0.522. The label is 1, so the loss would shrink if the output rose. Next: which of the 9 parameters should move, and by how much?

blocks.md: In practice we push a whole **mini-batch** through at once: stack $B$ examples as rows of a matrix $X$ and each layer becomes one matrix multiply $Z = X W^\top + b$, with a transpose because each example is now a row of $X$ instead of a column vector. Lesson 7 runs the backward pass in this form. That is why neural network training is dominated by matrix multiplication and runs well on GPUs.
Keep the cached values. The forward pass is not just for the prediction: the backward pass will reuse every $z^l$ and $a^l$ computed here, so frameworks store them.

blocks.question: An MLP maps a 784-pixel image through one hidden layer of 100 units to 10 class scores. How many parameters (weights plus biases) does it have?
blocks.explain: Layer 1: 784 x 100 weights + 100 biases = 78,500. Layer 2: 100 x 10 weights + 10 biases = 1,010. Total 79,510. Forgetting biases gives 79,400.

blocks.question: In the convention $z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l$, what is the shape of $W^2$ for that 784-100-10 network?
blocks.explain: $W^l$ has one row per unit in layer $l$ and one column per unit in layer $l-1$: 10 output units by 100 hidden units.

lessons.title: The chain rule on a computational graph

blocks.md:
Gradient descent needs $\partial L / \partial w$ for every parameter. The obvious approach is finite differences: nudge one weight by a small $\epsilon$, rerun the network and see how the loss changes. With a million weights that is a million and one forward passes per example (one baseline run plus one nudged run per weight), which is hopeless.

**Backpropagation** gets *all* the partial derivatives from one forward pass followed by one backward pass. It is the chain rule from calculus, applied in a careful order and reusing intermediate results.

Write the computation as a **computational graph**: each node is a simple operation (add, multiply, sigmoid), and edges carry values. Nodes are often called **gates**, as in a logic circuit. Each node only needs to know its **local gradient**: how its output changes with each of its inputs.

During the backward pass, a node receives the **upstream gradient** $\partial f / \partial \text{out}$ and multiplies it by each local gradient to get $\partial f / \partial \text{input}$. That product is the chain rule.

blocks.tex: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial q}\cdot\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}\qquad \text{(upstream gradient times local gradient)}

blocks.title: Backward pass through f = (x + y) z

scenes.caption: Forward pass with x = -2, y = 5, z = -4. The add node gives q = 3 and the multiply node gives f = -12.
Backward starts at the output with df/df = 1. From here, gradients flow right to left along the same edges.
Multiply node: the local gradient for each input is the *other* input. So df/dz = q = 3 and df/dq = z = -4. The multiply gate swaps its inputs.
Add node: both local gradients are 1, so it passes -4 unchanged to x and y. Check: raising x by 0.01 raises q to 3.01 and f to -12.04, a slope of -4.

blocks.md:
Three gates cover most of a neural network, and each has a simple backward rule:

- **Add** distributes the upstream gradient unchanged to every input (local gradient 1).
- **Multiply** sends each input the upstream gradient times the *other* input. A weight times an activation is a multiply, which is why $\partial L/\partial w$ involves the activation.
- **Max** routes the whole upstream gradient to the input that won in the forward pass and 0 to the others. ReLU is $\max(0, z)$, so it passes the gradient when $z>0$ and blocks it otherwise.

blocks.title: Staged backprop, one line per local gradient
blocks.code:
x, y, z = -2.0, 5.0, -4.0
q = x + y         # forward: add gate
f = q * z         # forward: multiply gate
df = 1.0          # backward starts at the output
dz = q * df       # multiply: other input times upstream
dq = z * df
dx = 1.0 * dq     # add: local gradient is 1
dy = 1.0 * dq

scenes.caption: The forward pass stores intermediate values (here q) because the backward pass needs them.
Seed the backward pass with the gradient of f with respect to itself.
Multiply gate: dz uses the cached q, dq uses z.
Add gate: copy dq to both inputs. Every gradient came from one backward sweep, in reverse order of the forward pass.

blocks.prompt: Now let one variable feed two places: $f = x \cdot x$ with $x = 3$, drawn as a multiply node whose two inputs are both $x$. Each branch gets 'the other input' times 1, which is 3. What is $df/dx$?
blocks.reveal: **6**, not 3. When a value is used in several places (a fork in the graph), the gradients coming back along each branch **add up**: 3 + 3 = 6, matching $d(x^2)/dx = 2x$. This is the multivariable chain rule, and it is why backprop code accumulates with `+=` instead of overwriting with `=`.

blocks.md: The same rule is what connects one hidden unit to many outputs. Say a hidden activation $h$ feeds two output units through weights 0.5 and -0.4, and the backward pass has already computed their errors $\partial L/\partial z_1 = 0.2$ and $\partial L/\partial z_2 = 0.5$. Each branch is a multiply gate, so it sends back the upstream gradient times the weight; then the two branches meet at $h$ and add.

blocks.title: Fan-out: one hidden unit feeding two outputs

scenes.caption: Forward: h is used twice, once by each output unit. That makes h a fork in the graph.
Backward has reached the outputs: dL/dz1 = 0.2 and dL/dz2 = 0.5.
Each branch applies the multiply rule: 0.5 x 0.2 = 0.1 along the top edge, -0.4 x 0.5 = -0.2 along the bottom.
The branches meet at h and add: dL/dh = 0.1 - 0.2 = -0.1. In lesson 5 this sum over every output a unit feeds becomes BP2, written as W transpose times the error vector.

blocks.md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

blocks.question: In the forward pass $m = \max(a, b)$ with $a = 4$ and $b = 1$. The upstream gradient is $\partial L/\partial m = 2$. What are $\partial L/\partial a$ and $\partial L/\partial b$?
options: 1 and 1
2 and 2
2 and 0
1.6 and 0.4, split by size
blocks.explain: Max routes the gradient: only the input that won (a = 4) affects m, so it gets the full upstream gradient 2. Nudging b slightly does not change m at all, so its gradient is 0.

blocks.question: Why is backpropagation so much cheaper than finite differences for a network with N weights?
options: It uses lower precision arithmetic
It only computes gradients for the last layer
It skips the forward pass
It reuses each node's upstream gradient for all of that node's inputs, so one backward pass of similar cost to the forward pass gives all N derivatives
blocks.explain: Finite differences need about N+1 forward passes because each one measures a single derivative. Backprop shares the work: a gradient computed once at a node is reused by everything upstream of it, so the full gradient costs a small constant times one forward pass.

lessons.title: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand

blocks.md:
Now apply the graph rules to a full network. The key bookkeeping quantity is the **error** of layer $l$, $\delta^l = \partial L/\partial z^l$: how the loss changes with each unit's pre-activation. Once you know $\delta^l$, every weight and bias gradient in that layer is one multiply away.

Nielsen's *Neural Networks and Deep Learning* packages this as four equations ($\odot$ is element-wise multiplication):

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned}\delta^L &= \nabla_{a^L} L \odot g'(z^L) &&\text{(BP1, output error)}\\ \delta^l &= \big((W^{l+1})^\top \delta^{l+1}\big) \odot g'(z^l) &&\text{(BP2, pass error back)}\\ \partial L/\partial b^l_j &= \delta^l_j &&\text{(BP3)}\\ \partial L/\partial W^l_{jk} &= a^{l-1}_k\, \delta^l_j &&\text{(BP4)}\end{aligned}
blocks.caption: BP1: output error equals the loss slope for each output times the activation slope. BP2: a layer's error equals the next layer's error sent back through the transposed weights, times the local slope. BP3: bias gradient equals error. BP4: weight gradient equals input activation times error.

blocks.md: Each equation is the chain rule. In BP1, the first factor is the gradient of the loss with respect to the output activations (the nabla symbol), the vector of slopes $\partial L/\partial a^L_j$; since $a^L_j = g(z^L_j)$, multiplying by $g'(z^L_j)$ turns it into $\partial L/\partial z^L_j$. For BP2, unit $j$ of layer $l$ reaches the loss only through the next layer's pre-activations $z^{l+1}_k$, and each of those contains the term $W^{l+1}_{kj}\, g(z^l_j)$. So by the chain rule, $\delta^l_j$ is the sum over $k$ of $\delta^{l+1}_k$ times $W^{l+1}_{kj}$, times $g'(z^l_j)$, and a sum over the row index $k$ of $W_{kj}$ is exactly a multiply by $W^\top$. That sum is the fan-out rule from lesson 4: unit $j$ feeds every unit of the next layer, so their gradients add. For BP3 and BP4, look at $z^l_j = \sum_k W^l_{jk} a^{l-1}_k + b^l_j$: it grows by 1 per unit of bias and by $a^{l-1}_k$ per unit of $W^l_{jk}$, so those are the local gradients that multiply $\delta^l_j$.

Read them as graph rules. BP2 is the multiply gate run backwards: each unit in layer $l$ sends its activation forward along weights $W^{l+1}$, so the error comes back along the same weights, which is the transpose. Then it passes through the activation's local slope $g'(z^l)$. BP4 is the multiply gate again: a weight's gradient is the activation on its input side times the error on its output side. Biases are added, so BP3 just copies the error.

With a sigmoid output and cross-entropy loss, BP1 simplifies to $\delta^L = a^L - y$: as the ML fundamentals course showed for logistic regression, the sigmoid slope $a(1-a)$ cancels the denominator of the loss slope $(a-y)/(a(1-a))$, leaving prediction minus label. Multi-class outputs use **softmax**, which turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1; lesson 6 derives that with cross-entropy it gives the same form, the probabilities minus 1 at the true class.

blocks.title: Backward pass through the 2-2-1 network

scenes.caption: Same network and forward values as lesson 3 (L = 0.522). Edge labels show the weights; the backward pass will replace them with gradients.
BP1: output error = a - y = 0.594 - 1 = -0.406. Negative means raising the output's z would lower the loss.
BP4 for layer 2: dL/dW = hidden activation x output error. 0.611 x -0.406 = -0.248 and 0.622 x -0.406 = -0.253. Bias gradient (BP3) = -0.406.
BP2, step one: send the error back along the weights (W transpose). h1 gets 0.7 x -0.406 = -0.285; h2 gets -0.4 x -0.406 = +0.163, opposite sign because its weight is negative.
BP2, step two: multiply by the sigmoid slope a(1-a): 0.238 for h1 and 0.235 for h2. Hidden errors are -0.0677 and +0.0382, 6 to 11 times smaller than the output error.
BP4 for layer 1: input x hidden error. x1 = 1.0 gives -0.0677 and +0.0382; x2 = 0.5 halves them to -0.0338 and +0.0191. All 9 gradients done in one sweep.

blocks.prompt: The gradient for the weight from h2 to the output is -0.253, but that weight is -0.4. After a gradient descent step $w \leftarrow w - \eta\, \partial L/\partial w$ with learning rate $\eta = 0.5$, does the weight move toward 0 or away from it? Why does that help?
blocks.reveal: Toward 0: $-0.4 - 0.5 \times (-0.253) = -0.273$. h2 is active (0.622) and currently *pulls the output down* through a negative weight. The label is 1, so the output should go up; shrinking that negative pull does exactly that. Every gradient is negative for weights into the output, so the step raises the output regardless of the weight's current sign.

blocks.title: Updating W1 with one gradient step (learning rate 0.5)

scenes.caption: W1 before the step. Row j holds the weights into hidden unit j.
dL/dW1 is an outer product: hidden errors (-0.0677, 0.0382) times inputs (1.0, 0.5): entry (j, k) is error j times input k. Each row shares a sign because it shares one unit's error.
W1 - 0.5 x dW1. h1's weights rise, h2's fall, both by small amounts because the hidden errors were small.

blocks.md: After updating all 9 parameters with learning rate 0.5, rerunning the forward pass gives output 0.680 (up from 0.594) and loss 0.386 (down from 0.522). One example, one step, and the loss fell by about a quarter.

How do you know the gradients are right? **Gradient checking**: compare each analytic gradient (the one backprop computes from the formulas) with the centred difference $(L(w+h)-L(w-h))/(2h)$. Nudging both ways cancels the curvature term, so the estimate's error shrinks like $h^2$ instead of $h$. With $h = 10^{-5}$, the numerical estimate for $W^1_{11}$ is -0.0676539, matching the analytic value. To compare, use the **relative error** $|g_a - g_n| / \max(|g_a|, |g_n|)$, the gap between analytic and numerical gradients scaled by their size; the largest over all 9 parameters is about $7 \times 10^{-10}$. The CS231n notes treat relative errors above $10^{-2}$ as a probable bug and below $10^{-7}$ as good.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
x, y = np.array([1.0, 0.5]), 1.0
W1 = np.array([[0.5, -0.3], [0.2, 0.8]]); b1 = np.array([0.1, -0.1])
W2 = np.array([[0.7, -0.4]]);             b2 = np.array([0.2])

# forward (cache z and a for the backward pass)
z1 = W1 @ x + b1;  a1 = sig(z1)
z2 = W2 @ a1 + b2; a2 = sig(z2)
loss = -(y * np.log(a2) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - a2))

# backward
d2 = a2 - y                          # BP1 (sigmoid + cross-entropy)
dW2, db2 = np.outer(d2, a1), d2      # BP4, BP3
d1 = (W2.T @ d2) * a1 * (1 - a1)     # BP2
dW1, db1 = np.outer(d1, x), d1       # BP4, BP3

# one SGD step
lr = 0.5
W1 -= lr * dW1; b1 -= lr * db1; W2 -= lr * dW2; b2 -= lr * db2
blocks.caption: The whole worked example in NumPy. Printing loss, dW1 and dW2 after the backward section reproduces the figures above.

blocks.question: A hidden unit receives input $x_k = 0$ for this example. What is the gradient of the loss with respect to the weight from $x_k$ into that unit, for this example?
options: Equal to the unit's error delta
0, because BP4 multiplies the error by the input activation
Undefined
The same as the bias gradient
blocks.explain: BP4: $\partial L/\partial W_{jk} = a_k \delta_j$. If the input on that edge is 0, the weight had no effect on the output for this example, so its gradient is 0. The bias of the unit still gets $\delta_j$.

blocks.question: A colleague implements BP2 as `d1 = (W2 @ d2) * a1 * (1 - a1)` for a network where W2 has shape (10, 64). What happens?
options: It works, matrix order does not matter
It computes the gradient for the biases instead
It fails or computes garbage: the error must go back through the transpose, W2.T @ d2, giving one value per hidden unit
It only breaks when the batch size is 1
blocks.explain: W2 maps 64 hidden units to 10 outputs. Going backward, the 10 output errors must be distributed to 64 hidden units along the same connections: that is $(W^2)^\top \delta^2$, shape 64. W2 @ d2 is a shape error here, and for square matrices it silently produces wrong gradients, which a gradient check would catch.

blocks.question: Why were the hidden errors (about 0.07 and 0.04) so much smaller than the output error (0.406)?
options: The learning rate shrinks them
Hidden units always have smaller gradients by definition
Cross-entropy only affects the last layer
Each passed through a weight below 1 in size and a sigmoid slope of at most 0.25
blocks.explain: BP2 multiplies by the weight (0.7 or -0.4) and by $\sigma'(z) \approx 0.24$. That shrinkage per layer is harmless with one hidden layer but compounds with depth, which is the topic of lesson 9.

lessons.title: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient

blocks.md: Our network so far answers one yes-or-no question with one sigmoid output. A digit reader must pick one of 10 classes. The ML fundamentals course gave the recipe: one output unit per class producing a raw score, a **logit** (say 2.0 for cat, 1.0 for dog and 0.1 for bird), and **softmax** to turn the logits into probabilities by exponentiating each one and dividing by the total. Goodfellow et al. read logits as unnormalized log probabilities. Nielsen explains the name: multiply all logits by a large constant and the output tends to 1 for the largest logit and 0 for the rest, a hard maximum, so softmax is a softened max. New here: where its gradient comes from, and how it plugs into backprop.

blocks.caption: Softmax over the logits z, then cross-entropy on the true class y: the loss is minus the log of the probability given to the right answer.

blocks.title: Softmax and its gradient, step by step

scenes.caption: Logits z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]. They can be any real numbers, negative included, and need not sum to anything.
Exponentiate: e^2.0 = 7.389, e^1.0 = 2.718, e^0.1 = 1.105. All positive; the gaps grow because exp turns differences into ratios.
Divide by the total 11.21: p = [0.659, 0.242, 0.099], summing to 1. The loss is -ln 0.659 = 0.417.

Gradient on the logits, p minus one-hot(cat): [-0.341, 0.242, 0.099]. Bar heights show size, labels show sign. The true class is pushed up, the others down in proportion to their probability, and the three sum to 0.

blocks.md: Where does that gradient come from? First the **Jacobian** of softmax, the table of how each output $p_i$ moves when one logit $z_j$ moves. Write $S = \sum_k e^{z_k}$ so $p_i = e^{z_i}/S$, and note $\partial S/\partial z_j = e^{z_j}$. By the quotient rule, if $i = j$ the numerator also depends on $z_j$, giving $p_i - p_i p_j$; if $i \ne j$ only the denominator does, giving $-p_i p_j$. Both cases fit one formula using the **Kronecker delta** $\delta_{ij}$, which is 1 when $i = j$ and 0 otherwise.

blocks.tex: \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j} = -\frac{1}{p_y}\frac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_j} = -(\delta_{yj} - p_j) = p_j - \delta_{yj}
blocks.caption: Left: the softmax Jacobian. Right: chain it with L = -ln p_y. The 1/p_y from the log cancels the p_y in front of the Jacobian row, leaving probabilities minus the one-hot label.

blocks.md: So the output error is $\delta^L = p - \mathrm{onehot}(y)$, the same prediction-minus-label form you met for sigmoid in lesson 5. That is no coincidence: softmax over two logits $[z, 0]$ gives $e^z/(e^z + 1) = \sigma(z)$, so the sigmoid output is the two-class case. For the example above, centred differences on the loss (lesson 5's gradient check) match $[-0.341, 0.242, 0.099]$ to about $10^{-11}$. Nielsen's chapter 3 gets the same result: with a softmax output and this log-likelihood cost, the output bias gradient is $a^L_j - y_j$.

blocks.prompt: Recall the fix from the ML fundamentals course: subtract the largest logit $c$ first, which is exact because multiplying the top and bottom of softmax by $e^{-c}$ changes nothing. Now take logits $[0, -800]$, true class second. Compute the shifted softmax $p$, then $-\ln p_2$. What comes out?
blocks.reveal: `inf`, though the true loss is about 800. The shift changes nothing here (the largest logit is already 0), and $e^{-800}$ is smaller than the tiniest positive float64, about $4.9 \times 10^{-324}$ (that is $e^{-744.4}$), so it **underflows**: it rounds to exactly 0. Then $p = [1, 0]$ and $-\ln 0$ is infinite. The cure is never to form $p$ before taking the log. Work in log space, as the formula below does: $\ln p_2 = -800 - \ln(1 + e^{-800})$, which is $-800$ to every printed digit, an ordinary number.

blocks.tex: \ln p_y = z_y - c - \ln \sum_j e^{z_j - c}, \qquad c = \max_j z_j
blocks.caption: Log-softmax computed safely (the log-sum-exp trick). Every exponent is at most 0, so nothing overflows, and the largest term in the sum is exactly 1, so the log never sees 0.

blocks.md: The ML fundamentals course noted that PyTorch's `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` takes raw logits; now you can see why. PyTorch's optimization tutorial notes that it combines `nn.LogSoftmax` and `nn.NLLLoss`, so it computes log-softmax in the safe form above. For one output, `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss` folds the sigmoid into the loss and, in the docs' words, is more numerically stable than a sigmoid followed by `BCELoss` because it can use the log-sum-exp trick.

Misconception: raising one logit only raises its own probability. The Jacobian's off-diagonal entries $-p_i p_j$ are negative, so every other probability falls (they must still sum to 1). That is why a wrong class's logit gets the positive gradient $p_j$ even though the loss $-\ln p_y$ reads only the true class: $p_y$ depends on every logit through the softmax denominator.

Now give the lesson 3 network three outputs. Keep $W^1$, $b^1$ and the input $x = (1.0, 0.5)$, so the hidden activations are still 0.611 and 0.622, and replace the single output with a 3 x 2 matrix $W^2$ (rows $[0.7, -0.4]$, $[0.3, 0.5]$, $[-0.2, 0.1]$) and biases $b^2 = (0.2, 0, 0.1)$. The true class is A. Only BP1 changes; BP2 to BP4 run exactly as before.

blocks.title: One backward step through a 3-class softmax output

scenes.caption: Forward: each output unit takes a weighted sum of h1 and h2 plus its bias. The logits are 0.378, 0.494 and 0.040.
Softmax: p = [0.353, 0.396, 0.251]. The network currently prefers B, the wrong class. Loss = -ln 0.353 = 1.042.
BP1 for softmax: output error = p - onehot(A) = [-0.647, +0.396, +0.251]. No sigmoid slope appears; it cancelled in the derivation.
BP2, step one: each hidden unit sums the errors of all three outputs it feeds, weighted by its edges (W2 transpose). h1: 0.7 x -0.647 + 0.3 x 0.396 - 0.2 x 0.251 = -0.385. h2 gets +0.482.
BP2, step two: times the sigmoid slopes 0.238 and 0.235 gives hidden errors -0.0915 and +0.1133. A gradient check on all 15 parameters agrees to a relative error of 2e-10.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def log_softmax(z):
    c = z.max()                          # shift so the largest logit is 0
    return z - c - np.log(np.exp(z - c).sum())

sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
x, y = np.array([1.0, 0.5]), 0           # true class A = index 0
W1 = np.array([[0.5, -0.3], [0.2, 0.8]]); b1 = np.array([0.1, -0.1])
W2 = np.array([[0.7, -0.4], [0.3, 0.5], [-0.2, 0.1]]); b2 = np.array([0.2, 0.0, 0.1])

a1 = sig(W1 @ x + b1)
z2 = W2 @ a1 + b2
logp = log_softmax(z2)
loss = -logp[y]                          # 1.042

d2 = np.exp(logp); d2[y] -= 1           # BP1: p - onehot(y)
dW2 = np.outer(d2, a1)                   # BP4
d1 = (W2.T @ d2) * a1 * (1 - a1)         # BP2
dW1 = np.outer(d1, x)                    # BP4
blocks.caption: The 3-class step in NumPy. Rounded, d2 is [-0.647, 0.396, 0.251] and d1 is [-0.0915, 0.1133]. After one gradient step with learning rate 0.5, p for class A rises from 0.353 to 0.573 and the loss falls from 1.042 to 0.557.

blocks.question: A 10-class network gives the true class probability 0.98 and some wrong class probability 0.015. What are $\partial L/\partial z$ for those two logits?
options: 0 and 0, because the prediction is already right
blocks.explain: $\partial L/\partial z_j = p_j - \delta_{yj}$. True class: 0.98 - 1 = -0.02, a small push up. Wrong class: 0.015 - 0 = 0.015, a small push down. Confident correct predictions produce small gradients, but never exactly zero.

blocks.question: Your PyTorch model ends with `nn.Softmax(dim=1)` and you train it with `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()`. Loss goes down very slowly and never gets near 0. What is wrong?
options: CrossEntropyLoss needs one-hot targets
The learning rate is too high
Softmax is applied twice: CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and applies log-softmax itself
Softmax should be replaced by sigmoid for multi-class outputs
blocks.explain: The docs say the input is expected to contain unnormalized logits. Feeding probabilities (all between 0 and 1) applies softmax a second time to a narrow range of values, so with 10 classes the true class can get at most $e/(e+9) = 0.23$ and the loss can never drop below 1.46. Remove the Softmax layer and apply it only when you need probabilities at inference time.

lessons.title: Backprop for a mini-batch, in matrix form

blocks.md: So far every backward pass used one example as a column vector. Frameworks never train that way: as the tip in lesson 3 said, they stack $B$ examples as the rows of a matrix and run each layer as one matrix multiply. The backward pass has to follow. Take the same 2-2-1 network and three examples: lesson 3's $x = (1.0, 0.5)$ with $y = 1$, plus $(0.0, 1.0)$ with $y = 0$ and $(0.5, -0.5)$ with $y = 1$. Stacked, $X$ is a 3 x 2 matrix, one row per example, and $Y$ is 3 x 1.

blocks.tex: \underset{3\times2}{Z^1} = X W_1^\top + b_1,\quad A^1 = \sigma(Z^1),\quad \underset{3\times1}{Z^2} = A^1 W_2^\top + b_2,\quad A^2 = \sigma(Z^2),\quad L = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} L_i
blocks.caption: The batched forward pass. Each weight matrix keeps the course's shape (units out by units in), so the transpose appears because examples are now rows. The loss is the mean of the per-example losses.

blocks.md: Running it: row 1 reproduces lesson 3 exactly (output 0.594, loss 0.522), and the other two rows give outputs 0.562 and 0.617 with losses 0.825 and 0.484. The batch loss is their mean, 0.610. Now the backward pass, with the shape of every quantity written next to it.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} dZ^2 &= (A^2 - Y)/B &&3\times1 \\ dW_2 &= (dZ^2)^\top A^1 &&1\times2 \\ dA^1 &= dZ^2\, W_2 &&3\times2 \\ dZ^1 &= dA^1 \odot A^1 \odot (1 - A^1) &&3\times2 \\ dW_1 &= (dZ^1)^\top X &&2\times2 \\ db &= \text{column sums of } dZ \end{aligned}
blocks.caption: dZ means the gradient of L with respect to Z, a matrix the same shape as Z. Each line is BP1 to BP4 with a row per example.

blocks.md: Where do the transposes come from? For one example, BP4 says $dW_1 = \delta\, x^\top$, an **outer product**: a 2 x 1 column times a 1 x 2 row, giving one 2 x 2 matrix. With a batch, each example adds its own outer product. Write example $i$'s error as row $i$ of $dZ^1$ and its input as row $i$ of $X$. Entry $(j, k)$ of $(dZ^1)^\top X$ is $\sum_i dZ^1_{ij} X_{ik}$: error $j$ times input $k$, summed over the examples. So the matrix product *is* the sum of the per-example outer products, done in one call. The same move turns BP2's $W^\top \delta$ for one column into $dZ^2 W_2$ for a stack of rows.

blocks.title: dW1 is a sum of per-example outer products (x 1000)

scenes.caption: Cells show values x 1000. Example 1, x = (1.0, 0.5): its row of dZ1 is (-0.0226, 0.0127), lesson 5's hidden errors divided by B = 3. Its outer product with x is the first contribution.
Add example 2, x = (0.0, 1.0). Its x1 is 0, so it adds nothing to the first column (BP4 again: a zero input gives a zero weight gradient).
Add example 3, x = (0.5, -0.5). The total equals (dZ1) transpose times X computed in one matrix product, and a gradient check on all 9 parameters agrees to a relative error of 3e-10.

blocks.md: The biases follow the same logic. In the forward pass the single vector $b_1$ is added to every row of $XW_1^\top$; NumPy and PyTorch call this **broadcasting**. Copying one value into many places is a fork in the graph, and lesson 4 showed that gradients from the branches of a fork add up. So the bias gradient is the column sum of $dZ$: $db_1 = (-0.0111, 0.0084)$ here.

blocks.title: Shapes flowing backward through the batched network

scenes.caption: Forward shapes: X is 3 x 2 (examples by inputs), W1 is 2 x 2, the hidden layer 3 x 2, W2 is 1 x 2, the output 3 x 1. One number comes out: the mean loss.
Output error: dZ2 = (A2 - Y) / B, one value per example, so 3 x 1. Each gradient always has the shape of the thing it belongs to.
dW2 = dZ2 transpose times A1: (1 x 3) times (3 x 2) = 1 x 2, the shape of W2. The inner dimension 3 is the batch, summed away. dA1 = dZ2 W2 is (3 x 1)(1 x 2) = 3 x 2.
Through the sigmoid slope (element-wise, shape unchanged), then dW1 = dZ1 transpose times X: (2 x 3)(3 x 2) = 2 x 2, the shape of W1. Again the batch dimension is summed away.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
X = np.array([[1.0, 0.5], [0.0, 1.0], [0.5, -0.5]])   # B x 2
Y = np.array([[1.0], [0.0], [1.0]])                    # B x 1
W1 = np.array([[0.5, -0.3], [0.2, 0.8]]); b1 = np.array([0.1, -0.1])
W2 = np.array([[0.7, -0.4]]);             b2 = np.array([0.2])
B = len(X)

A1 = sig(X @ W1.T + b1)                  # B x 2
A2 = sig(A1 @ W2.T + b2)                 # B x 1

dZ2 = (A2 - Y) / B                       # B x 1  (mean reduction)
dW2, db2 = dZ2.T @ A1, dZ2.sum(0)        # 1 x 2, (1,)
dZ1 = (dZ2 @ W2) * A1 * (1 - A1)         # B x 2
dW1, db1 = dZ1.T @ X, dZ1.sum(0)         # 2 x 2, (2,)

# same thing, one example at a time
loop = sum(np.outer(dZ1[i], X[i]) for i in range(B))
print(np.allclose(dW1, loop))            # True
blocks.caption: Batched backprop for the 3-example batch. Rounded, dW1 is [[-0.0331, 0.0317], [0.0189, -0.0164]], and the per-example loop gives the same matrix.

blocks.prompt: PyTorch losses default to `reduction='mean'`. Suppose you switch to `reduction='sum'` and keep the learning rate. With a batch of 64, what happens to each update step?
blocks.reveal: Every gradient becomes **64 times larger**, because the $1/B$ in $dZ^2 = (A^2 - Y)/B$ is gone and it flows into every layer's gradient. The same learning rate now takes steps 64 times as big, which can easily diverge. To get identical updates, divide the learning rate by $B$. With the mean, each step uses the average of the per-example gradients, the minibatch gradient of the ML fundamentals course, so its expected size is the same whatever $B$ is; `'mean'` is also the default the PyTorch loss docs list.

blocks.md: A batched gradient is the per-example gradient summed (or averaged) over the rows of the batch. The transposes are just how a matrix product writes that sum, and a quick check that every gradient has the shape of its parameter catches most mistakes.

Conventions differ. The course stores $W$ as units out by units in, so a layer is $Z = XW^\top$ and $dW = dZ^\top X$. CS231n's neural network case study stores $W$ as inputs by outputs, so a layer is $Z = XW$ and its code reads `dW = np.dot(X.T, dscores)`. Same sums, transposed bookkeeping. Justin Johnson's CS231n handout on derivatives shows how to find either form: work out a tiny case on paper, then read off the pattern.

blocks.question: A layer has $W$ of shape 64 x 784 (course convention, units out by units in), the batch $X$ is 32 x 784 and $dZ$ is 32 x 64. Which expression gives $dW$?
options: `X.T @ dZ`
`dZ @ W`
`dZ.T @ X`
`dZ @ X.T`
blocks.explain: $dW$ must be 64 x 784, the shape of $W$. Only `dZ.T @ X`, (64 x 32)(32 x 784), produces that, summing over the 32 examples. `X.T @ dZ` gives 784 x 64, the transposed convention. `dZ @ W` is the gradient for the layer's input $X$, and `dZ @ X.T` does not even have matching inner dimensions.

blocks.question: Why is the bias gradient the sum of $dZ$ over the batch, rather than, say, its first row?
options: The same bias vector is added to every example's row, so it affects every example's loss, and the gradients from those uses add up
Because biases are not multiplied by anything
Summing is an approximation that saves memory
Because PyTorch requires it
blocks.explain: Broadcasting copies $b$ into all $B$ rows, which is a fork: one value used in $B$ places. By the fan-out rule, the gradients from all uses add. Taking only one row would ignore how the bias affected the other examples.

lessons.title: The cost of backprop: compute, activation memory, checkpointing

blocks.md: **Compute cost.** Most of the work is matrix multiplies. For a layer $Z = XW^\top$ (batch $X$), backprop needs two products of the same size as the forward one: $dX = dZ\,W$ to keep the error moving, and $dW = dZ^\top X$ for the update. These are the batched BP2 and BP4 from lesson 7. So the backward pass costs roughly twice the forward pass, and a full training step about three forward passes. Nielsen's looser statement is that backprop costs about as much as two forward passes; either way it is a small constant, not a factor of N.

**Memory cost.** The backward pass for layer $l$ needs $a^{l-1}$ and $z^l$ from the forward pass, so every layer's activations stay in memory until that layer's backward step runs. Activation memory grows with depth and batch size, and during training it can exceed the memory used by the weights. You can trade compute for memory by recomputing activations instead of storing them: Chen et al. (2016) do this to train an $n$-layer network with $O(\sqrt{n})$ activation memory for roughly one extra forward pass. The trick, now called **gradient checkpointing**: split the $n$ layers into $\sqrt n$ segments of $\sqrt n$ layers each, store only the activations at segment boundaries, and during the backward pass recompute one segment's activations at a time. Memory holds about $\sqrt n$ boundaries plus one segment of $\sqrt n$ layers, hence $O(\sqrt n)$.

blocks.title: Why activations must stay alive until backward

scenes.caption: Simplified model: forward costs 1 unit per layer and backward 2 (two matrix multiplies). During the forward pass each layer's input is stored.
Loss is computed, then backward runs in reverse. Layer 3's backward step is the first to use its stored input a2, which is freed right after.
The first layer's input is needed last, so it is held for the whole step. Peak memory is at the forward/backward turn, when every activation is alive.

blocks.prompt: A 100-layer network is trained with gradient checkpointing in 10 segments of 10 layers. At the peak of the backward pass, about how many layers' activations are in memory, compared with 100 without checkpointing?
blocks.reveal: About **20**: the 10 stored segment boundaries, plus the 10 layers of the one segment currently being recomputed and backpropagated. That is the $\sqrt n + \sqrt n$ count from Chen et al. with $n = 100$. The price is recomputing each segment's forward pass once, roughly one extra forward pass in total.

blocks.md: Backprop's compute is a small constant times the forward pass, about two more matrix multiplies per layer. Its memory is the real constraint: every activation from the forward pass stays alive until its layer's backward step, unless you pay compute to recompute it.

blocks.question: You double the batch size and the run now goes out of GPU memory, even though the model's weights are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weights are copied once per example
Backprop needs a second copy of the loss
Stored activations for the backward pass scale with batch size
Gradients scale with batch size while weights do not, and gradients are the bulk
blocks.explain: Weights and their gradients have a fixed size. Activations kept for the backward pass scale with batch size times depth, so they grow. Remedies: a smaller batch, gradient checkpointing (recompute instead of store), or lower precision activations.

lessons.title: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds

blocks.md: In lesson 5 the hidden errors came out 6 to 11 times smaller than the output error after passing back through a single layer. That shrinkage happens again at every layer, and in a deep network it compounds.

**Vanishing gradients.** BP2 multiplies the error by $g'(z)$ at every layer on the way back. The sigmoid slope is at most 0.25, so the slope factors alone shrink the signal by at least 4 times per layer: after 10 layers that is at most $0.25^{10} \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-7}$. Early layers then barely learn. Glorot and Bengio (2010) found the sigmoid poorly suited to deep networks with random initialisation because it can drive the top hidden layer into saturation, where the slope is near 0.

The figure below draws random starting weights with a spread tied to the layer width $n$. The reason: a unit's pre-activation adds up $n$ terms $w_k a_k$. With independent, zero-mean weights of variance $v$, the sum's variance is $n v$ times the inputs' mean square, so $v = 1/n$, a standard deviation of $1/\sqrt n$, keeps the signal's scale steady from layer to layer. The backward pass has the mirror condition: BP2 sums $n_{\text{out}}$ terms $W_{kj}\delta_k$, so keeping the error's scale steady needs $n_{\text{out}} v = 1$. **Glorot** (or Xavier) initialisation, from Glorot and Bengio's paper, takes $v = 2/(n_{l-1} + n_l)$, two over the input width plus the output width, a compromise between the two conditions. **He** initialisation uses $v = 2/n$ for ReLU, doubling the variance because ReLU zeroes about half of its inputs.

blocks.title: Weight gradient size per layer, relative to the last layer

scenes.caption: Simulated 8-layer sigmoid net, 64 units per layer, weights drawn with standard deviation 1/sqrt(64), random upstream gradient. Layer 1's weight gradients are about 0.00007 of layer 8's.

Same net with ReLU and He initialisation (standard deviation sqrt(2/64)), one random draw. Slope 1 for active units and the init keep signal scale steady, so every layer gets a gradient of similar size (here 1.0 to 1.33 times layer 8).

blocks.md: The reverse problem, **exploding gradients**, happens when the per-layer factors are larger than 1, often because weights are too large. Both are why initialisation schemes (Glorot, He) scale random weights by the layer width, and why ReLU-family activations replaced sigmoid in hidden layers. The next course, Training deep nets in practice, covers initialisation and these training techniques in depth.

scenes.caption: A 2-4-1 net (tanh hidden, sigmoid output, cross-entropy, full-batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.5), biases 0, weights drawn from NumPy's default_rng(1) standard normal. Before training: predictions near 0.5, loss 0.671.
After 100 steps: loss 0.123. The outputs have already moved toward the targets.
After 2,000 steps: loss 0.0024. Backprop found weights that solve XOR, with no hand design.

Same code with default_rng(0), after 2,000 steps: loss stuck near 0.349. It fits (0,0) and (1,0) but outputs about 0.5 for the other two. Gradient descent stalled in a poor region of the loss surface.

blocks.md: Backprop computes the exact gradient of the loss at the current weights; it does not guarantee a good solution. The loss surface of a network is not **convex** (bowl-shaped, so that every valley is the lowest one), so the starting point matters. Lesson: always check the loss curve, and try more than one seed.

blocks.question: In an 8-layer sigmoid network, training loss falls slowly and you find the first layer's weights have barely changed. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Use ReLU activations with He initialisation
Increase the number of training epochs only
Add more sigmoid layers
Remove the biases
blocks.explain: The cause is repeated multiplication by small sigmoid slopes (at most 0.25) in BP2. ReLU has slope 1 for active units and He initialisation keeps the signal scale stable, as the bars figure showed. More epochs only wait longer; more sigmoid layers make it worse.

blocks.question: A layer has 256 inputs and 64 outputs. Which weight variance does Glorot initialisation use, and which condition does each width come from?
options: $1/256$: only the forward pass matters
$2/320 = 1/160$: 256 from keeping activations steady going forward, 64 from keeping errors steady going backward
$2/64$: He initialisation for the output width
$1/64$: only the backward pass matters
blocks.explain: Forward, a unit sums 256 inputs, so steady activations need $256\,v = 1$. Backward, BP2 sums over the 64 units each input feeds, so steady errors need $64\,v = 1$. Glorot averages the widths: $v = 2/(256 + 64) = 1/160$.

lessons.title: Build it: a tiny autograd engine from scratch

blocks.md:
Every gradient in this course so far came from the same two moves: give each node its local gradient rule, then visit the nodes in reverse order, multiplying and adding. Both moves are mechanical, which means a program can do them. In this lesson you write that program, about 60 lines of Python, and check it against PyTorch.

The tiny example is lesson 4's $f = (x + y)z$ with $x = -2$, $y = 5$, $z = -4$. By hand, $df/dx = df/dy = -4$ and $df/dz = 3$. The engine should find the same numbers without being told the formula.

**Autograd** is short for automatic differentiation: the framework derives the gradients from the code you ran. In PyTorch, every operation on a **tensor** (PyTorch's multi-dimensional array) with `requires_grad=True` records its backward function in a graph during the forward pass; `loss.backward()` walks that graph in reverse and **accumulates** gradients into each parameter's `.grad`. Andrej Karpathy's [micrograd](https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd) implements the same **reverse-mode** engine (reverse mode means applying the chain rule from the output back toward the inputs, which is backprop) for scalars in about 100 lines. The version below follows its design.

The design has one class, `Value`, wrapping a single number. Each `Value` stores its `data`, a `grad` that starts at 0, the `parents` it was computed from, and a small function `_backward` that knows the local rule of the operation that created it. Overloading `+` and `*` means ordinary Python expressions build the graph as a side effect: writing `q = x + y` creates a node `q` whose parents are `x` and `y`.

blocks.code:
import math

class Value:
    def __init__(self, data, parents=()):
        self.data, self.grad = data, 0.0
        self.parents = parents          # nodes this one was computed from
        self._backward = lambda: None   # pushes self.grad to the parents

    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data + other.data, (self, other))
        def _backward():                # add: local gradient 1
            self.grad += out.grad
            other.grad += out.grad
        out._backward = _backward
        return out

    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other))
        def _backward():                # multiply: the other input
            self.grad += other.data * out.grad
            other.grad += self.data * out.grad
        out._backward = _backward
        return out

    def backward(self):
        order, seen = [], set()
        def visit(v):                   # parents always land first
            if v not in seen:
                seen.add(v)
                for p in v.parents:
                    visit(p)
                order.append(v)
        visit(self)
        self.grad = 1.0
        for v in reversed(order):       # output first, leaves last
            v._backward()
blocks.caption: Part 1: the core. Each operation returns a new Value and attaches a closure (a function that remembers the variables around it) holding the gate rule from lesson 4. backward() sorts the graph so that every node comes after its parents, then runs the closures from the output back.

blocks.title: The engine computing df/dx for f = (x + y) z
blocks.code:
x, y, z = Value(-2.0), Value(5.0), Value(-4.0)
q = x + y               # q.parents = (x, y)
f = q * z               # f.parents = (q, z)
f.backward()
# inside backward():
order = [x, y, q, z, f] # from visit(f): parents first
f.grad = 1.0
f._backward()           # mul: q.grad += z.data * f.grad
                        #      z.grad += q.data * f.grad
z._backward()           # leaf: nothing to do
q._backward()           # add: x.grad += q.grad
                        #      y.grad += q.grad
y._backward()           # leaf
x._backward()           # leaf

scenes.caption: Forward: each operation creates a Value and records its parents. Nothing about derivatives has happened yet, but the graph now exists.
backward() first orders the graph: visit(f) visits q, which visits x and y, then z. Each node is appended only after its parents, so reversing the list puts f first.
Seed the output with df/df = 1, as in lesson 4.
f's closure runs the multiply rule: each input gets the other input's value times f.grad.
z is a leaf (no parents), so its _backward is the empty default. q's closure runs the add rule and copies q.grad to both parents.
The leaves do nothing. Every gradient matches the hand computation from lesson 4.

blocks.md: Two details carry all the weight. First, every rule uses `+=`, never `=`. For `g = a * a` with `a = 3`, the multiply closure adds 3 for the left input and 3 for the right, and both land on the same object, so `a.grad` ends at 6, the fan-out rule from lesson 4. Second, the order. A node's closure pushes its `grad` to its parents, so it must run only after *every* node that uses it has finished adding into that `grad`. Visiting in reverse **topological order** (an ordering of a graph's nodes in which every node comes after all the nodes it depends on) guarantees exactly that.

blocks.prompt: Take `x = Value(1.0)`, `a = x * x`, `b = a * 2`, `c = a + b`, so $c = 3x^2$ and $dc/dx = 6$. Set `c.grad = 1` and run the closures in the order c, a, b instead of the topological c, b, a. What is `x.grad`?
blocks.reveal: **2.0**, not 6. When `a._backward()` runs, `a.grad` holds only the 1 that `c` sent; `b` has not yet added its 2. So `a` passes $2x \times 1 = 2$ to `x`. Then `b` raises `a.grad` to 3, but too late: nothing propagates it again. Topological order makes `a` wait until both of its users, `b` and `c`, are done.

blocks.caption: Part 2: more methods for the Value class body. Each is a one-input rule with a known local slope: power, tanh (1 - tanh squared, lesson 3), exp (itself) and log (1/x). Subtraction and division are built from add, multiply and power, so need no rules of their own.

blocks.code:
import random
random.seed(1)
X = [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]
Y = [0, 1, 1, 0]
W1 = [[Value(random.uniform(-1, 1)) for _ in range(2)] for _ in range(4)]
b1 = [Value(0.0) for _ in range(4)]
W2 = [Value(random.uniform(-1, 1)) for _ in range(4)]
b2 = Value(0.0)
params = [w for row in W1 for w in row] + b1 + W2 + [b2]

def forward(x):
    h = [(W1[j][0] * x[0] + W1[j][1] * x[1] + b1[j]).tanh() for j in range(4)]
    z = sum((W2[j] * h[j] for j in range(4)), b2)
    return 1 / (1 + (-z).exp())                       # sigmoid

def loss_fn():                                        # mean cross-entropy
    total = 0
    for x, y in zip(X, Y):
        p = forward(x)
        total = total - (y * p.log() + (1 - y) * (1 - p).log())
    return total / len(X)

for step in range(2001):
    for p in params:
        p.grad = 0.0                                  # zero before backward
    loss = loss_fn()
    loss.backward()
    for p in params:
        p.data -= 0.5 * p.grad                        # gradient descent
    if step in (0, 100, 2000):
        print(step, round(loss.data, 4))
blocks.caption: Part 3: a 2-4-1 network built from Value objects (tanh hidden units, sigmoid output, mean cross-entropy) trained on XOR with gradient descent, learning rate 0.5. Run after parts 1 and 2, it prints a loss of 0.6976 at step 0, 0.1037 at step 100 and 0.0024 at step 2000.

blocks.md: Is it right? Rebuilding the same network in PyTorch with the same starting weights, in float64, gives the same loss (0.69756) and all 17 gradients agree with the engine to within $10^{-16}$, which is rounding. One loss evaluation builds a graph of 252 `Value` nodes for just 17 parameters and 4 examples. micrograd's README says the same thing about its scalar engine: each neuron is chopped into all of its individual tiny adds and multiplies. Frameworks keep the identical bookkeeping but make each node a whole tensor operation, so a matrix multiply is one node whose backward rule is the batched formula from lesson 7.

Gradients accumulate across calls too. In this engine, `backward()` resets only the output's grad, so calling it twice on `f = x * x` with `x = 3` leaves `x.grad` at 12, not 6. That is why part 3 zeroes every parameter's grad before each backward pass, and why PyTorch training loops call `opt.zero_grad()`.

blocks.code:
import torch

X = torch.tensor([[0., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 0.], [1., 1.]])
y = torch.tensor([[0.], [1.], [1.], [0.]])
model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(2, 4), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(4, 1))
loss_fn = torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()   # sigmoid + cross-entropy
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.5)

for step in range(2000):
    opt.zero_grad()            # gradients add up unless reset
    loss = loss_fn(model(X), y)
    loss.backward()            # backprop fills p.grad for every parameter
    opt.step()                 # p = p - lr * p.grad
blocks.caption: The same XOR training loop with PyTorch autograd: the graph, the closures and the topological walk are hidden inside loss.backward(). Exact numbers depend on PyTorch's own random initialisation.

blocks.md: The idea is old. Efficient reverse-order chain-rule computation appeared in control and sensitivity analysis in the 1960s and 1970s, Werbos proposed it for neural networks in 1981, and Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986) showed it learning useful hidden representations. Reverse mode is the right direction for training: forward-mode differentiation carries derivatives from the inputs toward the output and needs one pass per input, while reverse mode needs one pass per output, and a network has millions of weights but a single scalar loss (Baydin et al., section 3).

blocks.question: A training loop calls `loss.backward()` and `opt.step()` every iteration but never calls `opt.zero_grad()`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, backward overwrites .grad each time
Each step uses the sum of all gradients so far, so updates grow and point in stale directions
The graph is freed, so the second backward raises an error
Weights stop changing after the first step
blocks.explain: PyTorch accumulates into `.grad` (the `+=` rule for forks, applied across calls). Without zeroing, step t applies the sum of gradients from steps 1 to t. The official tutorial calls zero_grad every iteration to avoid this double counting.

blocks.question: You add a `relu` method to `Value` with `out = Value(max(0, self.data), (self,))`. Which closure is correct?
options: `self.grad = out.grad`
`self.grad += out.grad`
`self.grad += (self.data > 0) * out.grad`
`self.grad += max(0, out.grad)`
blocks.explain: ReLU is the max gate: it passes the upstream gradient when the input was positive and blocks it otherwise, and like every rule it must accumulate with `+=`. micrograd's own relu uses the same test on its output, `(out.data > 0) * out.grad`. Option 4 clips the *gradient*, which is a different (wrong) operation.

lessons.title: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits

blocks.md:
Every network in this course so far trained on one to four examples. Time for real data. **MNIST** is a set of handwritten digits: as Nielsen describes it, 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images, each 28 by 28 pixels in greyscale, scanned from samples written by US Census Bureau employees and high school students. The task: look at an image, say which digit 0 to 9 it shows.

The network is the one from lesson 3's quiz: flatten each image into 784 numbers, a hidden layer of 100 ReLU units, and 10 output logits, 79,510 parameters in all. The loss is softmax cross-entropy from lesson 6.

Following Nielsen, hold back 10,000 of the training images as a **validation set**: data the network never trains on, used to watch for overfitting and choose settings, as in the ML fundamentals course. The 10,000 test images are scored once at the end. Training uses mini-batches of 64, plain SGD with learning rate 0.1, and 10 **epochs**, where an epoch is one full pass over the 50,000 training images, 782 updates.

blocks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

torch.manual_seed(0)
data = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True,
                      transform=transforms.ToTensor())
train, val = torch.utils.data.random_split(data, [50000, 10000])
train_dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
val_dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(val, batch_size=1000)
train_eval = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train, batch_size=1000)

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(),            # 28 x 28 to 784
                      nn.Linear(784, 100), nn.ReLU(),
                      nn.Linear(100, 10))      # 10 logits
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()                # softmax + cross-entropy
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

def evaluate(dl):
    with torch.no_grad():
        n = loss = right = 0
        for X, y in dl:
            out = model(X)
            loss += loss_fn(out, y).item() * len(y)
            right += (out.argmax(1) == y).sum().item()
            n += len(y)
    return loss / n, right / n

print("start: val loss %.3f acc %.3f" % evaluate(val_dl))
for epoch in range(10):
    for X, y in train_dl:
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X), y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    print(epoch + 1, "train loss %.3f acc %.3f" % evaluate(train_eval),
          "| val loss %.3f acc %.3f" % evaluate(val_dl))

blocks.prompt: Before any training step, the network outputs nearly equal logits for all 10 classes. What loss should the first evaluation print?
blocks.reveal: About $\ln 10 = 2.303$. Equal logits give each class probability 0.1, and the loss is $-\ln 0.1$. This run printed **2.300**, with accuracy 0.080 (chance is 0.1). The CS231n notes recommend exactly this sanity check: a starting loss far from $\ln(\text{number of classes})$ points to a bug or a bad initialisation.

blocks.title: Loss during training: hidden layer vs no hidden layer

scenes.caption: After epoch 1 (782 SGD steps), the MLP is already at 0.295 training loss, 91.6% validation accuracy. The linear model (logistic regression, no hidden layer) is at 0.366.
Epoch 5: the MLP's loss went up from epoch 4 (0.138 to 0.173). SGD on small mini-batches is noisy, so the loss need not fall every epoch. Judge the trend, not one point.
Epoch 10: MLP 0.063 training and 0.100 validation loss, 97.1% validation accuracy. The linear model is nearly flat at 0.273 and 0.292: it is short of capacity, not of time.

blocks.md: Read the gap, too. The MLP's validation loss (0.100) sits above its training loss (0.063), and the gap widened as training went on: the network is starting to fit details of the training images that do not carry over. For the linear model the two lines stay close (0.273 and 0.292), because it is too simple to memorise much. On the untouched test set the MLP scores **97.2%** and the linear model **92.2%**. That is 278 wrong answers instead of 779 out of 10,000: one hidden layer cut the error rate by about 2.8 times.

Diagonal set to 0 so the mistakes show. The biggest: 17 fours read as nines and 15 sevens read as twos, then 9 each for sevens as nines, eights as sixes and nines as fours. These are pairs that look alike when written quickly.

blocks.md: What did the hidden units learn? Row $j$ of the first weight matrix has 784 entries, one per pixel, and unit $j$'s pre-activation is the dot product of that row with the image. So the row can be drawn as a 28 x 28 picture, a **template**: the unit responds strongly to images with ink where its weights are positive and little ink where they are negative. Nobody designed these templates. Backprop shaped them from the training labels alone.

Hidden unit 87: a vertical stroke of positive weight through the middle, with negative weight on both sides. Each unit is a learned feature detector; the output layer combines 100 of them, as the XOR network combined two.

blocks.md: Nothing new happened here. The forward pass, softmax cross-entropy, BP1 to BP4 in batched form and the SGD step are the same ones you ran by hand on a 2-2-1 network; MNIST just has 79,510 parameters and 64 examples per batch.

Use the test set once. If you pick the number of epochs, the learning rate or the hidden size by looking at test accuracy, the test set has become a validation set and its score is no longer an honest estimate. Choose with the validation set, then report test.

blocks.question: You train a 10-class classifier and the very first loss printed is 9.7. What does that most likely tell you?
options: Training is going well; high loss means room to improve
The initial logits are far from uniform (for example, weights initialised too large), or the loss is computed wrongly
The dataset has more than 10 classes
The learning rate is too small
blocks.explain: With small random weights the logits are nearly equal and the loss should be about $\ln 10 = 2.30$. A much larger value means the network starts out confidently wrong, typically from oversized initial weights, or there is a bug such as applying the loss to the wrong tensor. Check this before training.

blocks.question: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss has stopped falling and is slowly rising. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Train for many more epochs until validation loss falls again
Report test accuracy at every epoch and pick the best one
Increase the model size
Stop at the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping) or add regularisation
blocks.explain: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is the signature of overfitting. Early stopping or weight decay from the ML fundamentals course address it. Picking the epoch by test accuracy leaks the test set into model selection.

blocks.question: The linear model's training and validation losses both flattened near 0.27 to 0.29 by epoch 10. What would help it most?
options: Adding a hidden layer with a nonlinearity, as the MLP does
Training for 100 more epochs
A larger learning rate
A bigger validation set
blocks.explain: Both curves flat and close together means underfitting: the model lacks capacity. A linear model can only draw hyperplanes between classes (lesson 1). The hidden layer adds the bends, which is why the MLP reached 0.063 and 0.100 on the same data.
